# SFCmodel


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

The SFCmodel class holds the model equations and solver.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/slevey087/SFCmodeler/blob/main/SFCmodeler/SFCmodel.py#L22"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### SFCmodel

``` python
def SFCmodel(
    equations:NoneType=None, redundant_equation:NoneType=None, start_period:str='2000', freq:str='Y'
):
```

First create the terms using
[`Parameter`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/term.html#parameter)
and
[`Variable`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/term.html#variable)
and [`Random`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/term.html#random),
and then create a model by writing equations in a list, using `<<` as
the equals sign:

``` python
Variable.default_value = 10

C = Variable("C","Consumption")
T = Variable("T","Taxes")
V = Variable("V","Wealth",100)
Y = Variable("Y","GDP")

alpha1 = Parameter("alpha_1","MPC out of income",0.6)
alpha2 = Parameter("alpha_2","MPC out of wealth",0.4)
G = Parameter("G","Government spending",5)
theta = Parameter("theta","Tax rate",0.2)
```

``` python
model = SFCmodel(
    [
        C << alpha1 * (Y - T) + alpha2 * V(-1),
        Y << C + G,
        T << theta * Y,
        V << V(-1) + Y - T - C
    ]
)
```

Optional additional arguments include a redundant equation, and a start
and period length for the time index (which defaults to yearly begining
with 2000).

``` python
model = SFCmodel(
    [
        C << alpha1 * (Y - T) + alpha2 * V(-1),
        Y << C + G,
        T << theta * Y,
        V << V(-1) + Y - T - C
    ],
    redundant_equation = V << V(-1) + G - T,
    start_period="2020",
    freq="Y"  # these are pandas PeriodIndex strings
)
```

If you have not already set inital_values on the
[`Variable`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/term.html#variable)s
and
[`Parameter`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/term.html#parameter)s,
you can set them on the
[`SFCmodel`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/modeler.html#sfcmodel),
either one at a time:

``` python
model[Y] = 10
```

``` python
model[Y]
```

    10.0

``` python
model.data[V].iloc[-1].squeeze()
```

    np.float64(100.0)

Or as a whole set using “:” and a `dict` (or anything that will parse to
one):

``` python
model[:] = {
 C: 10.0,
 G: 5.0,
 T: 10.0,
 V: 100.0,
 V(-1): 100.0,
 Y: 10.0,
 alpha1: 0.6,
 alpha2: 0.4,
 theta: 0.2
}
```

``` python
# This will work too
model[:] = [
 (C, 100.0),
 (G, 50.0),
 (T, 100.0),
 (V, 1000.0),
 (V(-1), 1000.0),
 (Y, 100.0),
 (alpha1, 0.7),
 (alpha2, 0.3),
 (theta, 0.1)
]
```

Quickly get a text-presentable `dataframe` overview of what you just set
using `.inventory()`:

``` python
model.inventory()
```

The redundant equation refers to the accounting identity that is
overdetermined, as typical in SFC models. If you specify it, then the
solver will check that it holds (within solver error) every period, and
warn you if not. You can also check it manually using
`.check_redundant_equation`:

``` python
model.check_redundant_equation()
```

    {'lhs': 100.0, 'rhs': 95.0, 'inside tolerance': False}

In this case the check fails because our default values are not
consistent (though that won’t matter for this model, because the
equations don’t look back to the values of these variables from previous
periods).

`.solve()` runs the solver for the (optional) specified number of
periods, and returns the results

``` python
model.solve()   # solves one period
model.solve(3)  # solves 3 more periods
```

      0%|          | 0/1 [00:00<?, ?it/s]

      0%|          | 0/3 [00:00<?, ?it/s]

`model.data` is an instance of
[`ModelResults`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/modelresults.html#modelresults),
which is a thin wrapper around a pandas `DataFrame`, but which allows
for some fancy slicing and indexing. See [that
page](./02_modelresults.ipynb) for more details.

One more useful way to inspect the data is with `.equation_values()`,
which will return the data for all the terms in the equation for the
specified variable (also as
[`ModelResults`](https://slevey087.github.io/SFCmodeler/modelresults.html#modelresults))

``` python
model.equation_values(C)
```

*C* = *α*<sub>1</sub>(−*T* + *Y*) + *α*<sub>2</sub>*V*<sub>−1</sub>

The easiest way to shock a variable is to assign it a new value and then
run the solver again:

``` python
model[alpha1] = 0.7

model.solve(4)
```

``` python

```

    {'converged': [], 'not converged': [C, T, V, Y]}

Instead of specifying a certain number of periods to solve, you can also
ask the solver to find the **steady state** of the model, using the
`steady` argument:

``` python
model.solve(100, steady=True);
# The number 100 becomes give_up_steps, with the solver searching for a steady state but stopping after give_up_steps.
```

      0%|          | 0/100 [00:00<?, ?it/s]

Under the hood, the steady state checker calls `.check_steady_state`,
which uses `np.isclose` to compare the last two timesteps (comparing
growth rates for variables declared with `growth=True`).

Instead of `steady=True`, you may also pass a `dict` that can specify a
list of variables to `ignore`:

``` python
# rewind the clock:
model.data = model.data[:"2028"]

model.solve(100, steady={'ignore':[C, T]});
```

      0%|          | 0/100 [00:00<?, ?it/s]

You can also include any `kwargs` to `np.isclose` in the `steady` `dict`
(or in arguments to `check_steady_state()` if you want to call it
manually), but specify `rol_g` and `atol_g` as `rtol` and `atol` for the
growth variables.
